toc.label: See it on a real home
Why Irvine is not one market

pillars.intro:
At nine in the morning in Woodbury, filtered through the paseo trees, Alabaster looks like the warmest, calmest white you have ever seen. At two in the afternoon on a west-facing slope in Orchard Hills, the same paint on the same wall reads yellow.

Nothing changed except the light. That is the problem with choosing an exterior color the way almost everyone chooses one — from a two-inch card, indoors, under a showroom bulb, for a decision that will sit on the front of your house for the next eight years.

This guide walks the six villages of Irvine and what each one does to color. It is the same walk we take with homeowners before anything is scheduled.
pillars.viz_intro: Before reading further, try it. Pick a style direction and tap through the palettes — the home below re-paints itself in real time. It is a demonstration of the same thing our design team does with your actual elevation during a complimentary consultation: you see the color on the house before a single gallon is tinted, instead of imagining it from a swatch.

why_different.heading: Why Irvine Is Not One Market
why_different.body:
People say "Irvine" as though it were a single place with a single look. It is not. The villages were built in different decades by different builders in different architectural languages, and they sit at different elevations with genuinely different exposure.

The value spread alone is roughly five to one, from Stonegate’s close-set Santa Barbara streetscapes to Hidden Canyon’s guard-gated canyon estates. Three of the six are gated. Each runs its own design review, and Orchard Hills alone has three separate associations.

A palette that looks considered in one village can look borrowed in the next.

pillars.villages_intro: Architecture, light, and the palettes that actually hold in each one.

villages.name: Orchard Hills
villages.body:
Orchard Hills sits against the ridge, and that changes everything about color. Warm stucco, stone wainscots and clay tile all take direct afternoon sun, and a white that looked composed at nine in the morning can read distinctly yellow by two. Streets like Summerland and Glacier Valley run along slopes where west-facing elevations get the worst of it.

The village is three separate associations — The Groves, The Reserve and The Summit — each with its own board and its own design review. That matters more than most homeowners expect when a color change is on the table.

villages.name: Altair
villages.body:
Altair is the one village where the architecture, not the light, sets the rule. Broad uninterrupted stucco planes and deep fascias mean there is nowhere for a mediocre finish to hide — roller stipple and lap marks that would vanish on a textured Mediterranean facade are obvious across twenty feet of flat wall.

The streets are named for astronomy. Bellatrix is a star in Orion, Chasma is a planetary canyon, Bolide is a bright meteor, and Sagan Way needs no explanation. The community itself is named for the star Altair. A palette here should feel deliberate and modern rather than warm and traditional.

villages.name: Portola Springs
villages.body:
Most Portola Springs homes are still wearing some version of the palette the builder chose for the entire street. That makes a repaint the single highest-impact change available here — and also the easiest to get wrong, because Mediterranean stucco reacts unpredictably to warm whites under bright foothill light.

Streets run botanical: Yellow Iris, Soaring Eagle, Campion. The village steps up toward Loma Ridge, so elevation and exposure vary noticeably from one block to the next.

villages.name: Hidden Canyon
villages.body:
Hidden Canyon is the most valuable village in Irvine by a factor of two, and the smallest. Smooth-troweled stucco and limestone on canyon-edge lots means the finish is judged from three feet, not thirty — every patch, pinhole and lap line is visible if the preparation was not right.

The canyon gives you two different light conditions in one day: cool, often marine-influenced mornings, then hot open afternoons. A white that feels refined at noon can go noticeably cold by evening. Panorama and Shady Arbor are the streets you will see on listings.

villages.name: Woodbury
villages.body:
Woodbury is the largest village on this list and the one where light works differently. Mature landscaping and garden paseos keep much of the community filtered and cool through the day, which flatters warmer whites that would go brassy on an exposed hillside. Vintage, Great Lawn, Sarabande and Chantilly are typical of its streets.

It is also the kitchen village. Woodbury was built out around 2005, which means solid cabinet boxes wearing dated finishes — the exact case where refinishing beats replacing.

villages.name: Stonegate
villages.body:
Stonegate streets are tight, immaculate and close enough together that one repaint visibly resets the standard for the block. Coleridge, Dunmore, Doverwood and Fenway are close-set Santa Barbara facades where your neighbours will notice the result whether or not they say so.

That proximity is also a practical constraint. Zero-setback elevations mean overspray risk on a neighbour’s car, wall and planting, so containment and wind-checked scheduling matter more here than anywhere else in Irvine.

common.heading: What Every Irvine Repaint Has in Common
common.body:
The villages differ. The work underneath does not.

On stucco, everything you can see at the end was decided before a drop of color went on. Rolling a full exterior is faster for the crew; spraying and back-rolling is better for the house, because it drives the coating into the texture instead of leaving it sitting on top.
points: Pressure wash, then stucco crack and patch repair floated to match the existing texture
Bonding primer on any bare substrate — not a shortcut worth taking on inland exposure
Sherwin-Williams Emerald and Duration, two coats at full wet-mil, never over-thinned
Graco and Titan airless application, back-rolled on stucco, hand-cut at every transition
Your community association’s design review package prepared as part of the project
Raking-light inspection at the end, then a 2-Year Warranty on labor and materials

cost.heading: What It Costs
cost.answer: VIP exterior work in Irvine starts at $4.75 per square foot of paintable surface — the premium end of a local market that runs roughly $2.74 to $4.89. Every estimate is itemized line by line: preparation, primer, coating, trim and accents priced separately, never a single lump sum.
cost.body:
Paintable surface is not the same as your home’s square footage. It is the actual area being coated — walls, fascia, trim, eaves — which on a two-story stucco home usually runs somewhere near the interior figure but is measured on site rather than assumed.

We sit at the premium end and say so plainly. The argument for it is not craftsmanship in the abstract; it is that a repaint done twice costs the whole amount again.

seo.meta_title: What Does It Cost to Paint a House in Irvine? | VIP Painting
seo.meta_desc: Irvine exterior painting runs about $2.74–$4.89 per square foot. The five things that decide where your home lands, and what an itemized estimate covers.

cluster.intro:
Two homes on the same Irvine street, same builder, same floor plan, built the same year. One quote comes back at the low end of the market. The other comes back several thousand dollars higher. Neither painter is trying to take advantage of anyone.

The difference is almost never the paint. It is five things, and only one of them is visible from the curb.

answer.label: The short answer
answer.body: Exterior painting in Irvine, California runs roughly $2.74 to $4.89 per square foot of paintable surface based on published local rate data. VIP Home Painting starts at $4.75 per square foot of paintable surface, at the premium end of that range. Where a specific home lands inside the range is decided by five variables, in rough order of impact:
points: Paintable surface area — which is not the same number as your home’s square footage
Substrate condition — how much crack repair, patching and priming the stucco needs before any color goes on
Number of colors in the scheme — body, trim, fascia, doors and accents are separate cut-ins, not one pass
Height and access — second stories, hillside lots and zero-setback elevations all change the labor
Coating specification — product line, film thickness, and whether the crew back-rolls or only sprays

sections.heading: Paintable surface is not your square footage
sections.body:
This is the single most common misunderstanding, and it is the reason two quotes on the same house can look like they are describing different projects.

When a listing says a home is 3,200 square feet, that is conditioned interior floor area. Paintable surface is something else entirely — the actual area a brush or sprayer has to cover. Exterior walls, fascia, eaves and soffits, trim, garage doors, railings, shutters. It is measured elevation by elevation on site.

A two-story home with tall entry volumes and deep overhangs can have far more paintable surface than a single-story home of the same interior footage. A home with extensive stone or brick wainscot can have considerably less. Neither is knowable from a listing.
sections.callout: If a quote arrives without anyone having measured your elevations, it is an estimate of a house in general, not of your house.

sections.heading: What the stucco is hiding
sections.body:
On stucco — which is most of Irvine — everything you can see when the job is finished was decided before a drop of color went on.

Hairline cracking is normal on stucco and does not mean anything is structurally wrong. But every crack has to be opened, filled and floated to match the surrounding texture, or it telegraphs straight through the new coating within a season. A home with substantial crack repair carries real hours that a home with sound stucco does not.

The same is true of bare substrate. Anywhere the previous coating has failed, chalked or been repaired needs bonding primer before topcoat. This is the line item most likely to be quietly missing from a cheaper bid, and it is the one that decides whether the finish lasts eight years or three.
list: Pressure wash to remove chalking, dust and organic growth
Crack repair opened, filled, and floated to match existing texture
Bonding primer on all bare or repaired substrate
Caulking at every transition, penetration and dissimilar-material joint

sections.heading: How many colors are actually in the scheme
sections.body:
A single-color repaint and a four-color scheme are not the same job, even on the same house.

Every additional color is a separate mobilization: separate masking, separate cut-in by hand, separate dry time before the adjacent surface can be worked. A body-and-trim scheme is standard. Add a contrasting fascia, a front door in a third color, and shutters or a garage door in a fourth, and the labor rises noticeably even though the material cost barely moves.

This is worth knowing before you fall in love with a five-color elevation. It is not that it cannot be done well — it is that it should be priced honestly as what it is.

sections.heading: Height, slope, and how close the neighbors are
sections.body:
Labor is the majority of any exterior repaint, and access is what decides how much labor a given square foot takes.

Second-story elevations mean staging, ladders or lifts, and slower, more careful work. Hillside lots — much of Orchard Hills sits against the ridge — can mean a downhill elevation that needs scaffolding to reach at all. And in tighter villages like Stonegate, where homes sit close together with minimal setback, containment is not optional. Overspray onto a neighbor’s car, wall or planting is a genuine risk, which means more masking, more shielding, and scheduling around wind rather than against it.

None of that shows up in a square-foot number. All of it shows up in the hours.

sections.heading: The specification, and what "two coats" actually means
sections.body:
Two bids can both say "two coats" and describe meaningfully different work.

Coating applied too thin, or over-thinned to spray more easily, technically leaves two coats on the wall and delivers a fraction of the intended film thickness. Manufacturers publish a wet-mil spec for a reason. Applying below it is the most invisible way to reduce cost on a painting job, and the homeowner does not find out for several years.

The other variable is method. Spraying alone is faster. Spraying and then back-rolling drives the coating into the stucco texture instead of leaving it bridging on top of it, which is what adhesion and service life depend on. It takes longer, and it is the correct way to do it.
sections.callout: VIP specifies Sherwin-Williams Emerald and Duration, two coats at full wet-mil, never over-thinned — sprayed and back-rolled on stucco with Graco and Titan airless equipment.

table.heading: What an itemized estimate should show you
table.intro: Every VIP estimate is broken out line by line rather than presented as a single number. That is partly transparency and partly self-defense: a lump sum is impossible to compare against another bid, and it is where scope quietly disappears.
rows: Pressure wash, crack repair, patching, sanding, scraping of failed coating
Age and condition of existing stucco
Bonding primer on bare, repaired or chalking substrate
How much of the wall is exposed after prep
Transitions, penetrations, window and door perimeters
Number of openings and material joints
Two coats at full wet-mil, sprayed and back-rolled
Paintable surface area and access height
Hand cut-in, separate color, separate pass
Linear footage and number of colors
Garage doors, entry door, shutters, railings, ironwork
How many accent colors are in the scheme
Masking, shielding, landscape and hardscape protection
Setback distance and proximity to neighbors
Design review package prepared for your community association
table.note: Typical project totals are deliberately not published here. A total is only meaningful once the elevations have been measured, and a number invented for a web page is worth nothing to you.

takeaways.heading: What to remember
points: Ask for the paintable surface measurement, not a price based on your home’s square footage.
Ask what happens to cracks and bare substrate specifically. Vague answers here are the most expensive kind.
Ask whether the crew back-rolls on stucco or only sprays.
Ask for the estimate itemized. If two bids are far apart, the difference is almost always a line one of them left out.
Count the colors in your scheme before comparing quotes — a four-color elevation is a different job from a two-color one.

faq.q: How much does it cost to paint a house in Irvine?
faq.a: Published rates for Irvine, CA run roughly $2.74 to $4.89 per square foot of paintable surface. VIP Home Painting starts at $4.75 per square foot of paintable surface, at the premium end of that range. The final figure depends on paintable surface area, the condition of the existing stucco, how many colors are in the scheme, access and height, and the coating specification.

faq.q: How do your prices compare to other contractors?
faq.a: VIP sits at the premium end of the Irvine range and says so plainly rather than competing on price. The argument for it is not craftsmanship in the abstract — it is that a repaint done twice costs the whole amount again. Every estimate is itemized line by line so it can be compared honestly against any other bid.

faq.q: Why is one painting quote so much cheaper than another?
faq.a: Almost always because of something that was left out rather than something that was discounted. The most common omissions are bonding primer on bare substrate, crack repair floated to match texture, and back-rolling on stucco. All three are invisible on the day the job finishes and decisive three years later. Comparing itemized estimates rather than totals is the only reliable way to see the difference.

faq.q: What is paintable surface, and why not just use my square footage?
faq.a: Paintable surface is the actual area being coated — exterior walls, fascia, eaves, soffits, trim, garage doors and railings — measured elevation by elevation on site. Your home’s square footage is conditioned interior floor area, which is a different number. A two-story home with tall entry volumes can have far more paintable surface than a single-story home of the same interior footage.

seo.meta_title: Why Exterior Paint Colors Look Wrong on the House | Irvine
seo.meta_desc: A two-inch swatch is not the same color on 2,000 square feet of Irvine stucco. The four reasons why, and how to be certain before you commit to a repaint.

toc.label: See it on a real home

cluster.intro:
The card is two inches wide. It is printed on flat paper. You are looking at it indoors, under a fluorescent fixture, holding it next to four other cards that are also two inches wide.

The wall is two thousand square feet of textured stucco in full Southern California sun, next to a clay tile roof you are not replacing and a stone wainscot you are not touching.

These are not the same color, and they were never going to be.

answer.label: The short answer
answer.body: An exterior paint color chosen from a swatch frequently looks wrong on the finished house for four reasons that are all predictable and none of which are the painter’s fault:
points: Scale — the same pigment reads dramatically more saturated across a large surface than on a small card
Light — direction, time of day and surrounding reflected color shift how a paint appears, and in Irvine that shift is severe
Texture — stucco casts thousands of micro-shadows that paper does not, which reads visually darker
Fixed elements — roof tile, stone, hardscape and window frames are not changing, and the new color has to live with them

sections.heading: The same color is a different color at scale
sections.body:
This is a well-documented perceptual effect and it catches almost everyone. A hue viewed across a large area appears more intense and more saturated than the identical hue viewed on a small sample. A beige that looked restrained on a card can read distinctly gold across an entire elevation. A soft gray-green can arrive at full strength as something closer to sage.

The practical consequence: people routinely choose one to two steps stronger than they meant to, discover it at the moment the crew pulls the masking, and then have to decide whether to live with it or pay for the whole job again.

sections.heading: Irvine light is not one light
sections.body:
The villages of Irvine sit at different elevations with genuinely different exposure, and that does more to your color than most homeowners expect.

In Woodbury, mature landscaping and garden paseos keep much of the community filtered and cool through the day, which flatters warmer whites that would go brassy elsewhere. On a west-facing slope in Orchard Hills, that same warm white takes direct afternoon sun off the ridge and reads yellow. Hidden Canyon gives you two different conditions in a single day — cool, often marine-influenced mornings, then hot open afternoons — so a white that feels refined at noon can go noticeably cold by evening.

Same paint. Same wall. Different hour, different village, different color.
sections.callout: A color is not a property of the paint. It is a property of the paint, the surface, the light, and everything nearby that is reflecting into it.

sections.heading: Stucco is not paper
sections.body:
A paint chip is a flat, smooth, matte printed surface. A stucco wall is a landscape of peaks and valleys, and every one of them casts a small shadow.

The visual result is that the same color reads meaningfully deeper on stucco than on the card, and the effect gets stronger the heavier the texture. A smooth-troweled finish, like much of Hidden Canyon, behaves differently again — it holds the color closer to true, which is precisely why any imperfection in the preparation is visible from three feet.

Sheen compounds it. The same color in a higher sheen picks up more directional light and appears to shift through the day, while a flatter finish holds steadier but shows surface irregularity more readily.

sections.heading: The things you are not repainting decide more than you think
sections.body:
Your roof is staying. So is the stone wainscot, the driveway, the window frames, and in most Irvine villages a good deal of hardscape and mature planting.

Every one of those surfaces reflects color back onto the wall. A terracotta tile roof throws warm light down onto the fascia and upper body all day. Large expanses of green landscaping push a subtle cool cast onto shaded elevations. A warm-toned stone base can make a neutral gray body read faintly lilac by contrast — an effect nobody predicts from a card and everybody notices on the finished house.

This is the failure mode that produces the most regret, because the color is not wrong in isolation. It is wrong next to the four things that were always going to stay.

sections.heading: What getting it wrong actually costs
sections.body:
A wrong exterior color is not a touch-up. It is the entire project again — full preparation, full material, full labor — because the surface has to be recoated in its entirety for the finish to be uniform.

For a typical Irvine home that is four to seven thousand dollars, paid a second time, plus another stretch of weeks with the house staged and the crew on site. And in a design-review community it can also mean a second submittal to the association.

Against that, the cost of being certain in advance is thirty minutes.

cluster.viz_intro: This is the point. Pick a style direction below and tap through the palettes — the home re-paints itself in real time. It is a demonstration of what our design team does with your actual elevation during a complimentary consultation: you see the color on the house, in context, before a single gallon is tinted.

takeaways.heading: What to remember
points: Expect any color to read stronger and deeper on the house than on the card. Almost everyone chooses a step too strong.
Judge a candidate color at three different times of day, on the elevation that actually faces the sun.
Hold it against the roof, the stone and the hardscape — the things you are not repainting are half the decision.
A repaint to fix a color is the whole project again, not a touch-up.
The only reliable test is seeing it on your own house before anything is scheduled.

faq.q: Why does my paint look different on the wall than it did on the swatch?
faq.a: Four reasons, all predictable. Scale makes a color read more saturated across a large surface than on a small card. Light direction and time of day shift how the pigment appears. Stucco texture casts micro-shadows that make the color read deeper than it does on flat paper. And fixed elements you are not repainting — roof tile, stone, hardscape, landscaping — reflect their own color back onto the wall.

faq.q: Should I paint a test patch on the house first?
faq.a: A large sample board moved around the elevations through the day is far better than judging from a card, and better than a small patch painted directly on the wall, which is influenced by the color already underneath it. The limitation of any physical sample is that it still shows you a fragment rather than the whole house. Rendering your actual elevation in the candidate palettes shows you the finished result, which is the thing you are actually deciding on.

faq.q: How much does it cost to repaint if I choose the wrong color?
faq.a: It costs the entire project again — roughly four to seven thousand dollars for a typical Irvine exterior — because the surface has to be fully recoated for the finish to be uniform. It is not a touch-up. In a design-review community it may also require a second submittal to the association.

faq.q: Does the roof really affect what exterior color I should choose?
faq.a: Substantially. A terracotta or clay tile roof reflects warm light onto the fascia and upper body of the house throughout the day, which pushes neutral colors warmer than they appear in isolation. Since the roof is not changing, it is one of the fixed constraints the color has to work with rather than a detail to consider afterward.

seo.meta_title: Irvine HOA Exterior Paint Color Approval — How It Works
seo.meta_desc: Find your association, understand who decides, and submit once. A practical guide to exterior color approval across the six villages of Irvine, CA.

toc.label: The mistake that costs a round

cluster.intro:
Most exterior color applications in Irvine are not rejected. They are returned — for a missing document, an unclear sample, or a submittal sent to the wrong body entirely. Each return costs weeks, and the weeks are the part homeowners actually mind.

The process is not difficult. It is just specific, and it differs by village.

answer.label: The short answer
answer.body: Exterior color changes in Irvine’s master-planned villages generally require written approval from the community association’s architectural or design review body before work begins. Getting through in one round comes down to four steps:
points: Identify the exact association that governs your property — several Irvine villages contain more than one
Obtain that association’s current architectural guidelines and treat them, not general advice, as the authority
Submit a complete package the first time, with the colors clearly identified by manufacturer name and code
Do not start work until written approval is in hand, regardless of how routine the change seems

sections.heading: Step one: find out which association actually governs your home
sections.body: This sounds trivial and it is where a surprising number of submittals go wrong. The City of Irvine publishes an official lookup tool that maps a property to its homeowners association and management company. It is a government primary source, and it is more reliable than a listing site, a neighborhood forum, or the assumption that your village has one association. Start at cityofirvine.gov/community-development/irvine-homeowners-associations.
sections.callout: Orchard Hills is not one association. The Groves, The Reserve and The Summit each have their own board and their own review. Submitting to the wrong one costs you the full cycle.
list: Orchard Hills — multiple separate associations, each with its own board
Stonegate — Stonegate Village Owners Association (SVOA). Note that a separate, unrelated 126-unit "Stonegate Homeowners Association, Inc." exists elsewhere; they are not the same entity
Woodbury — Woodbury Community Association, one of the largest in Irvine at 4,067 units
Portola Springs — Portola Springs Association
Altair — Altair Irvine Master Association
Hidden Canyon — self-presented at livinghiddencanyon.com

sections.heading: Step two: the guidelines are the authority, not anyone’s advice
sections.body:
Every association sets its own architectural standards, and they are not interchangeable between villages — or, in Orchard Hills, between associations inside the same village.

Request the current architectural guidelines and the CC&Rs from your management company in writing, and read the section on exterior modifications before you fall in love with a palette. What is approvable in one Irvine village may not be in the next, and guidelines are revised periodically, so a neighbor’s successful submittal from four years ago is not a reliable guide.

Anyone who tells you what your HOA will accept without having read your association’s current guidelines is guessing. That includes painters.

sections.heading: Step three: what to have ready before you submit
sections.body:
Requirements vary by association, so the guidelines you obtained in step two govern. That said, applications generally turn on being able to show the reviewers precisely what they are approving — which means unambiguous color identification and a clear picture of the result.

The items below are what VIP assembles as part of the project, at no additional cost. If you are managing the submittal yourself, they are a reasonable starting checklist to compare against your association’s actual form.
list: The association’s current architectural application form, completed in full
Every color identified by manufacturer, name and code — for example Sherwin-Williams Alabaster SW 7008 — never by description alone
Physical color samples or manufacturer chips, as the guidelines specify
A clear indication of which color goes on which element: body, trim, fascia, garage door, entry door, accents
Photographs of the existing elevations
A rendering of the proposed colors on your actual home, where the association accepts one
Contractor license and insurance information, if the form requests it

sections.heading: The mistake that costs most people a round
sections.body:
It is not choosing a bold color. It is submitting something the committee cannot evaluate with confidence.

A reviewer looking at three paper chips stapled to a form has to imagine the result on your elevation, in your village’s light, next to your roof. Faced with genuine uncertainty, a committee’s safest decision is to ask for more information — which is a return, and another cycle.

Giving them the finished picture removes that uncertainty. It is the same reason the visualization matters to you: the difference between a decision made on imagination and a decision made on sight.

The second most common mistake is starting work before written approval arrives. Verbal encouragement from a board member is not approval, and unwinding unapproved work is far more expensive than waiting.

takeaways.heading: What to remember
points: Confirm your exact association through the City of Irvine lookup before anything else.
Get the current guidelines in writing. They are the authority; a neighbor’s old approval is not.
Identify every color by manufacturer, name and code, and say which element each one goes on.
Submit complete the first time — returns cost weeks, not days.
Never start work before written approval is in hand.

faq.q: Do I need HOA approval to repaint my house in Irvine?
faq.a: In Irvine’s master-planned villages, exterior color changes generally require written approval from the community association’s architectural or design review body before work begins. Requirements are set by each association individually, so the governing document is your own association’s current architectural guidelines. Confirm which association governs your property using the City of Irvine homeowners association lookup.

faq.q: How do I find out which HOA my Irvine home belongs to?
faq.a: The City of Irvine publishes an official lookup tool that maps a property to its homeowners association and management company, at cityofirvine.gov/community-development/irvine-homeowners-associations. This matters more than it sounds: several Irvine villages contain more than one association. Orchard Hills alone includes The Groves, The Reserve and The Summit, each with its own board and review process.

faq.q: Does VIP Home Painting handle the HOA submittal?
faq.a: Yes. Preparing your community association’s design review package is included as part of the project rather than charged separately. That covers identifying colors by manufacturer and code, documenting which color goes on which element, and providing a rendering of the proposed palette on your actual home where the association accepts one.

faq.q: What happens if I paint without approval?
faq.a: Associations can require unapproved work to be brought back into compliance, which in the case of exterior color means repainting the house at your own cost. Verbal encouragement from a board member or neighbor is not approval. Wait for the written decision — the delay is far cheaper than the alternative.

faq.q: How long does architectural approval take in Irvine?
faq.a: Timelines are set by each association and published in its own governing documents, so we will not quote a number that may not apply to your village. Request the review schedule and meeting calendar from your management company at the same time you request the guidelines. What is within your control is submitting a complete package the first time, since returns add a full cycle.

seo.meta_title: How to Choose Between White Exterior Paint Colors | Irvine
seo.meta_desc: Alabaster, Pure White, Snowbound, Greek Villa, Shoji White. Use LRV and undertone to tell them apart, then see the winner on your own Irvine home.

toc.label: See it on a real home

cluster.intro:
You have narrowed it to three whites. Side by side on the counter they are indistinguishable — three slightly different pieces of white paper.

On two thousand square feet of stucco, in Irvine sun, next to a clay tile roof, they are not remotely the same. One will look crisp and composed. One will go faintly yellow by mid-afternoon. One will read cold and slightly blue on the shaded elevation.

There are two published numbers that tell you most of this before you commit, and one way to be certain.

answer.label: The short answer
answer.body: To distinguish between white exterior paint colors that look identical on a chip, use three things in order:
points: Light Reflectance Value (LRV) — the manufacturer’s published 0–100 figure for how much light the color reflects. Higher reads brighter and flatter in strong sun; lower holds more depth and shows shadow
Undertone — the faint hue underneath the white, usually yellow, greige or gray. This is what decides whether it harmonizes with your roof and stone or fights them
Seeing it rendered on your own elevation — the only step that accounts for your village’s light, your texture, and everything you are not repainting

table.heading: Five whites people actually shortlist in Irvine
table.intro: These are Sherwin-Williams whites that appear repeatedly across the villages we work in. LRV is the manufacturer’s published Light Reflectance Value.
columns: Where it tends to hold in Irvine
rows: Contemporary elevations with broad flat planes — Altair
Filtered, shaded light — Woodbury’s garden paseos
Smooth-troweled stucco and canyon light — Hidden Canyon
Widely used; goes yellow on hot west-facing slopes
Bright foothill exposure where a high-LRV white would glare
table.note: LRV and undertone are the manufacturer’s published characteristics. Confirm against a current physical chip before finalizing, and treat any on-screen color as an approximation.

sections.heading: Read the LRV before you read the name
sections.body: Light Reflectance Value is a number from 0 to 100 describing how much visible light a color reflects. Pure black sits near 0; the brightest available whites approach the high 80s. Sherwin-Williams publishes an LRV for every color they make, and it is the most useful single number in the entire selection process. The reason it matters more outdoors than indoors is that exterior light is not adjustable. An LRV of 84 in full Irvine afternoon sun on a west-facing wall is genuinely bright — bright enough that architectural detail flattens out and shadow lines disappear. Drop to the mid-70s and the same elevation keeps its depth. The practical rule: the more direct sun an elevation takes, the more you should question a very high LRV. On a shaded or filtered elevation, high LRV is what keeps the house from looking dull.
sections.callout: Alabaster at 82 and Shoji White at 74 are only eight points apart on paper. On a sunlit stucco wall, that is the difference between crisp and glaring.

sections.heading: Find the undertone, because that is what will clash
sections.body:
No white is actually white. Every one has a faint hue mixed underneath — most commonly yellow, beige, greige or gray — and that undertone is invisible on a card and unmissable on a house.

The way to see it is by comparison, not in isolation. Put your candidates against a sheet of plain printer paper, which is close to a true white. The undertone that was invisible a moment ago becomes obvious: one card goes creamy, another goes distinctly cool.

Then hold them against the things you are not changing. A warm creamy white next to a terracotta tile roof reads harmonious. The same white next to cool gray slate can read dingy. A cool gray-undertoned white against warm stone can read faintly blue. This is where whites actually fail — not on their own merits, but against the fixed elements.
list: Warm undertone — Alabaster, Greek Villa. Harmonize with clay tile, terracotta, warm stone and wood
Cool undertone — Snowbound. Sits well with gray roofing, slate, black window frames and contemporary detailing
Near-neutral — Pure White. The most flexible, and the least forgiving of imperfect preparation
Greige — Shoji White. Reads as a white at a distance and as a warm neutral up close

sections.heading: Then see it on your own house, because the first two only narrow it
sections.body:
LRV and undertone will reliably get you from thirty candidates to three. They will not pick the winner, because neither number knows anything about your specific house.

They do not know your elevation faces west into afternoon sun coming off the Orchard Hills ridge. They do not know your roof is terracotta and throws warm light onto the fascia all day. They do not know your stucco carries a heavy texture that will read the color two steps deeper, or that your neighbor’s mature landscaping puts a cool cast on the north side every morning.

That is the gap the Custom Visualization Service closes. Our design team renders your actual home — your elevation, your roof, your surroundings — in each of the finalists, so the decision is made by looking rather than imagining. It costs nothing, it happens before anything is scheduled, and it takes about thirty minutes.

cluster.viz_intro: Try the principle here first. Pick a direction and tap through the palettes — the home below re-paints itself in real time so you can watch how much a small shift in undertone changes the whole elevation. Then we do it with your house.

faq.q: What is LRV and why does it matter for exterior paint?
faq.a: Light Reflectance Value is a manufacturer-published number from 0 to 100 describing how much visible light a color reflects, where 0 is black and the brightest whites reach the high 80s. It matters more outdoors than indoors because exterior light cannot be adjusted. A very high LRV on a west-facing wall in full Irvine sun can flatten architectural detail and wash out shadow lines, while a lower LRV keeps depth on the same elevation.

faq.q: How do I see the undertone in a white paint color?
faq.a: Compare it rather than viewing it alone. Hold the candidate against a sheet of plain printer paper, which is close to a true white — the undertone that was invisible in isolation becomes obvious, reading either creamy and warm or distinctly cool. Then hold it against your roof, stone and hardscape, since those fixed elements are what an undertone will either harmonize with or fight.

faq.q: What is the difference between Alabaster and Greek Villa?
faq.a: Both are warm whites with subtle yellow and beige undertones, but Greek Villa is published at LRV 84 against Alabaster at 82, so Greek Villa reads slightly brighter and Alabaster carries marginally more depth and creaminess. On a shaded or filtered elevation the difference is very subtle. In direct Irvine afternoon sun it is more apparent, and both can push yellow on a hot west-facing slope.

faq.q: Is Snowbound a warm or cool white?
faq.a: Cool. Sherwin-Williams describes Snowbound SW 7004 as having a slight gray undertone and pairing well with other gray-influenced colors. That makes it a reasonable choice alongside gray roofing, slate, black window frames and contemporary detailing, and a poor one next to warm terracotta tile, where its cool cast can read dingy by contrast.

faq.q: Which white is best for an Irvine home?
faq.a: There is no single answer, because the six villages of Irvine have genuinely different light. Woodbury’s filtered garden paseos flatter warmer whites that would go brassy on an exposed Orchard Hills slope, and Hidden Canyon’s cool marine mornings and hot open afternoons make a white behave differently across a single day. Narrow with LRV and undertone, then have the finalists rendered on your own elevation before deciding. Call (909) 312-5400 to arrange it.
